input: The performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. During that period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 18 °C, the approach was 3 K, and the range was 9 K. The approach describes how close the leaving water temperature comes to the wet-bulb temperature, while the range describes the temperature fall the water experiences as it passes through the tower. Together, these figures give a useful picture of how the tower performed under the conditions that prevailed during the logging period. It is important to note, however, that performance outside the logged month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures. Because a natural-draft tower depends on buoyancy-driven air flow, and because ambient conditions vary considerably between summer and winter, the summer results cannot simply be assumed to hold throughout the year. The choice of a summer month is itself relevant, since summer is when cooling duty is usually at its most demanding and when the wet-bulb temperature is at its highest. Performance recorded then represents the tower working under its most testing ambient conditions, although it cannot by itself reveal how the tower behaves across the rest of the year. Operators considering these results should therefore treat them as a characterisation of summer behaviour, and should be cautious about extrapolating them to the colder months, when both the heat load on the tower and the properties of the incoming air will be quite different in several respects. Results recorded in this way are most useful when they are read together with the conditions under which they were obtained, as this account sets out to do.
target: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 18 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 9 K. The approach is the difference between the leaving water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature; the range is the fall in water temperature across the tower. The two figures describe different parts of the tower's duty: the approach states how closely the cooled water comes to the limit the air sets, and the range states the cooling the water undergoes. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures. A natural-draft tower's driving force depends on the density difference the heated air creates, and that difference changes with the season; the summer figures therefore do not describe winter operation. The logged month fixes the tower's standing under summer conditions, and no figure in the passage extends beyond it. The logged month is the whole of the evidence. Within it, the wet-bulb temperature is a mean, and the approach and range are stated as the tower's performance over the same period; the passage does not give daily extremes, and no figure here describes the hottest days of the month. The tower is a natural-draft unit, so its air flow is set by the buoyancy of the warmed air rather than by a fan, and its performance follows the weather more closely than a mechanical-draft tower's would. For that reason the season is not a detail of the record but a condition of the figures: the same tower at winter wet-bulb temperatures would draw air differently, cool the water against a different limit, and return figures that this record cannot supply. The passage therefore reports a summer standing, complete for the month logged and silent beyond it. Nothing in the record is carried over to those conditions.
